transcript: Not only was this musical absolutely batshit insane, it also has some fascinating lore as an adaptation. Welcome to another episode of overthinking theater throwback, where I do retrospectives on recent theater history. Bat out of hell was a musical that premiered in 2017 in the UK, using songs by Jim Steinman, most of which were famously sung by meatloaf on the bat out of hell album. It was a very loose retelling of Peter Pan, which I'll say more about that in a minute. But like with Peter Pan elements, but set in this almost mad Max style dystopian cityscape where everyone rides motorcycles. And the musical was, to use the official dramaturgical terminology, fucking ridiculous. To say that it was over the top would be a gross understatement. In fact, the musical even incorporates the Jim Steinman quote about how if you don't go over the top, how are you gonna know what's on the other side? Wise words for us all in these trying times. And you know, people like to throw around words like campy or it knows what it is, but this show truly embodied that ethos by indulging in this seemingly deliberate stupidity to the point where it was kind of a wonder to behold. Probably my favorite example of this was during the Act 1 finale when they had confetti cannons go off at two different points in the same musical number. And speaking of, it was also quite the extravagant visual spectacle. With an almost operatic pageantry to the aesthetic and stage effects. And I didn't see it till it came to New York in 2019. I think I remember hearing that earlier versions in the UK had even more insane stagecraft that had to be cut for budget. But that. That didn't stop me from having the time of my freaking life at this show. I think about it all the time. But possibly even more fascinating is the unusual lore behind the show, which was a result of a daisy chain of adaptations that was longer and more complex than maybe any musical in history. Starts all the way back in 1969 when Jim Steinman was in college, and he wrote a musical called The Dream Engine. Then in 1974, he took elements of the dream engine, rewrote them, and reconceived it as kind of a loose adaptation of Peter pan. And that resulted in the musical Neverland, which played in DC in the spring of 1977. Unfortunately, the Neverland musical didn't really take flight either. But later that year in the fall of 1977, he reworked the material again, this time into the album Bat Out of hell, sung by meatloaf. The bat out of hell album spawned two sequels, bad out of Hell 2 back into hell and bad out of Hell 3. The monster is loose, and the 2017 musical essentially pulls songs from, I think, just the first two bad out of hell albums with some other Jim Steinman songs thrown in the mix. If you had trouble following that, no worries. I have a visual aid for you. I've always been fascinated by Peter Pan adaptations, and I like to joke that this is a loose retelling of a loose retelling of a loose retelling of Peter Pan. And I wouldn't have it any other way.
